teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
For five indexed observations and batch_size 2, a fixture with drop_last=False retains batches of sizes 2, 2 and 1. With drop_last=True, it retains two complete batches and discards the incomplete final batch. Retrieve each feature and target from the same observation index in __getitem__, and return them together. Test the batch boundaries and observed pairings under the declared shuffle policy rather than assuming a loader output's first position still corresponds to the source's first row. Also check __len__ against the sample count. The choice about the incomplete batch must appear in the fixture expectations, because counting three batches of size two would invent an observation.

Indexing defines correspondence before batching. If __getitem__ uses the feature at one index and the target at another, a loader can still collate a well-shaped but incorrectly paired batch. Test item identities as well as batch dimensions. The five-observation fixture also exposes the final partial-batch policy: retaining it gives one smaller batch, while dropping it changes how much of the dataset is consumed. Shuffle governs order, not whether a feature and its target remain the same item. Keep these responsibilities distinct so the expected loader output is tied to the dataset contract rather than assumed from its shape alone.

Draw or inspect the dimension chain for a single observation and then restore the leading minibatch dimension. Two features enter the first layer, three intermediate values emerge and one final output is produced; all four observations follow the same chain. Registered layer attributes make those layer parameters part of the module. The activation is elementwise, so it changes values without changing that intermediate width. Finally, compare the model output with the declared target/loss contract. The architecture example remains bounded to that contract rather than adding layers or final nonlinearities simply because they appear in another task.

required_facts.statement: Autograd records tensor operations as a computation graph and differentiates the scalar output through that graph using the chain rule.

source_refs: pytorch_learn_basics#autogradqs_tutorial.html — Tensors, Functions and Computational graph; Computing Gradients

required_facts.statement: For a linear batch Z = XW + b with scalar-loss derivative D = ∂L/∂Z, the chain rule yields ∂L/∂W = X.T @ D and ∂L/∂b = D.sum(axis=0), with any loss reduction already included in D.
source_refs: pytorch_learn_basics#autogradqs_tutorial.html — Tensors, Functions and Computational graph; Computing Gradients

teaching_blocks.content: A scalar loss must send the intended learning signal through the linear computation to its parameters. Autograd's result is inspectable: compare parameter gradients with a matrix-shaped chain-rule reference, not just with an expectation that backward should work.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Autograd records tensor operations as a computation graph and differentiates the scalar output through that graph using the chain rule. Backward accumulates into .grad, so clear old gradients before comparing a fresh computation with the reference.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: For a linear batch Z = XW + b with scalar-loss derivative D = ∂L/∂Z, the chain rule yields ∂L/∂W = X.T @ D and ∂L/∂b = D.sum(axis=0), with any loss reduction already included in D. Compare the computed gradients to the matrix-shaped chain-rule reference with explicit relative and absolute tolerances. Write assert predicate checks for the declared valid, boundary and failure cases; a false predicate raises AssertionError during ordinary non-optimized execution.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Take X=[[1, 2], [3, 4]] and the supplied derivative D=[[0.1], [0.2]] for Z=XW+b. The weight-gradient reference is X.T @ D = [[0.7], [1.0]], and the bias-gradient reference is [0.3]. Any loss reduction is already included in D; dividing again would change the reference. Set trainable leaf tensors to require gradients, form the scalar loss and call backward. Inspect .grad before clearing it, and compare shapes and values under explicit tolerances. For a fresh computation, clear the old gradients first because backward accumulates. Include a failure fixture whose gradient differs from the declared reference, not only a successful call.

Read the matrix reference one parameter at a time. The first weight combines feature values 1 and 3 with derivatives 0.1 and 0.2, giving 0.7. The second combines 2 and 4 with the same derivatives, giving 1.0. The bias combines derivatives over rows, giving 0.3. These shapes are part of the check: a transpose error can yield a different object even when some scalar values look plausible. Because D includes the loss reduction, use it once as supplied. Compare after backward and before clearing so the inspected gradients correspond to the intended fresh computation rather than zeroed or accumulated state.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Backward does not overwrite every old gradient automatically. A gradient comparison also needs the correct matrix shapes and reduction convention; a numerically plausible scalar is not the weight matrix reference.

The example adds 2 to a three-value tensor, squares the result, multiplies by 2, and takes the mean to produce a scalar. context.concept_name: Choose a task-compatible training loss

coverage.learning_objective: Choose a task-compatible loss and verify its output, target and gradient contracts.

required_facts.statement: A loss compares model outputs with the corresponding target representation; choose its input contract before computing the scalar objective.
source_refs: pytorch_learn_basics#optimization_tutorial.html — Hyperparameters; Loss Function; Optimizer; Full Implementation

required_facts.statement: CrossEntropyLoss expects unnormalized class logits; for class-index targets, logits have shape (N, C), targets have shape (N,) with dtype long and values in [0, C).

MSELoss takes input and target tensors of the same shape and, under mean reduction, sums squared elementwise differences and divides by M, the number of loss elements across all axes, not merely the number of examples.
BCEWithLogitsLoss combines sigmoid and binary cross-entropy for logits and same-shaped targets in [0, 1], rather than expecting already-sigmoid-transformed inputs.

For mean squared error over M output elements, the loss derivative with respect to an output is 2 × (output−target)/M, so its sign points toward increasing loss as the output moves away from the target.

For unweighted mean binary cross-entropy with logits over M loss elements across all axes, mean reduction divides the sum of element losses by M and the logit derivative is (sigmoid(logit)−target)/M; this distinguishes the probability representation from the raw logit.

For the unweighted mean class-index cross-entropy fixture with logits of shape (N, C), no ignored examples and no label smoothing, N is the number of examples: sum the per-example losses and divide by N, and compute each logit derivative as (softmax probability−one-hot target)/N.
Compute sigmoid(z) = 1 / (1 + exp(−z)), where exp is the exponential function, to convert each binary logit z to the probability used in the binary gradient reference.

For each row of C class logits, compute softmax probability p[c] = exp(z[c]) / sum_j exp(z[j]), summing over that row’s classes; torch.nn.Softmax(dim=1)(logits) performs this class-axis normalization for (N, C) logits.

The one-hot target row has 1 at the target class index and 0 at each other class; torch.nn.functional.one_hot(targets, num_classes=C) converts long class-index targets of shape (N,) to these rows of shape (N, C) for the manual gradient reference.

teaching_blocks.title: Gradients, Loss and Optimizer
teaching_blocks.content: The model output and target must meet the selected loss's contract. A scalar loss value alone cannot tell you whether class indices, logits, probabilities and same-shaped numerical targets were used correctly.

teaching_blocks.content: A loss compares model outputs with the corresponding target representation; choose its input contract before computing the scalar objective. CrossEntropyLoss expects unnormalized class logits; for class-index targets, logits have shape (N, C), targets have shape (N,) with dtype long and values in [0, C). MSELoss takes input and target tensors of the same shape and, under mean reduction, averages their squared elementwise differences.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: BCEWithLogitsLoss combines sigmoid and binary cross-entropy for logits and same-shaped targets in [0, 1], rather than expecting already-sigmoid-transformed inputs. For mean squared error over M output elements, the loss derivative with respect to an output is 2 × (output−target)/M, so its sign points toward increasing loss as the output moves away from the target. For unweighted mean binary cross-entropy with logits over M elements, the logit derivative is (sigmoid(logit)−target)/M; this distinguishes the probability representation from the raw logit.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content:
For the class-index cross-entropy fixture, assume unweighted mean reduction, no ignored examples and no label smoothing. N is the number of examples (rows) in logits of shape (N, C); C is the number of classes. Sum the per-example losses and divide by N. Each logit derivative is (softmax probability−one-hot target)/N.

Compute sigmoid(z) = 1 / (1 + exp(−z)), where exp is the exponential function, for each binary logit's probability. For each row of C class logits, softmax gives p[c] = exp(z[c]) / sum_j exp(z[j]); the denominator sums over classes in that row, not over examples. torch.nn.Softmax(dim=1)(logits) performs this class-axis normalization for (N, C) logits. A one-hot target row places 1 at the target class index and 0 elsewhere. torch.nn.functional.one_hot(targets, num_classes=C) converts long indices of shape (N,) to rows of shape (N, C) for the manual gradient reference.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
For an unweighted mean squared-error fixture with outputs [2, 4] and targets [1, 2], the loss is (1²+2²)/2 = 2.5 and output derivatives are [1, 2]. For a binary-logit fixture with one logit 0 and target 1, sigmoid(0)=0.5, so the supplied mean-logit derivative is −0.5. For target 1, decreasing the logit increases loss, while increasing it decreases loss. For a class-index task with three classes, verify logits width 3 and long target indices in [0, 3); use the stated softmax-minus-one-hot reference with its sample-count reduction. These are distinct output contracts, not interchangeable wrappers around arbitrary tensors.

Keep the mean-reduction factor visible in each reference. The two-element MSE fixture divides squared errors by two, while the one-element binary-logit fixture divides its sigmoid-minus-target derivative by one. A class-index cross-entropy reference subtracts the one-hot target from the softmax vector and divides by the sample count. Those equations support different target representations, so verify target dtype and axes before applying them. A positive-looking scalar loss is not proof of the right contract. Compare both value and derivative direction in the bounded fixture, retaining the supplied assumptions about unweighted mean reduction.

Trace the probability constructions before subtracting targets. In the binary fixture, M=1 loss element, so sigmoid(0)=1/(1+exp(0))=1/2, and (0.5−1)/1=−0.5. For an unweighted, unsmoothed class-index fixture with no ignored examples, take two rows of three zero logits and target indices [1, 2]. N=2 examples and C=3 classes. Each row's exponential values are [1, 1, 1], with denominator 3, so both probability rows are [1/3, 1/3, 1/3]. The one-hot rows are [0, 1, 0] and [0, 0, 1]. Subtract and divide by N=2 to obtain gradients [1/6, −1/3, 1/6] and [1/6, 1/6, −1/3].

```python
import torch

logits = torch.tensor([[0., 0., 0.], [0., 0., 0.]])
targets = torch.tensor([1, 2], dtype=torch.long)
probabilities = torch.nn.Softmax(dim=1)(logits)
one_hot = torch.nn.functional.one_hot(targets, num_classes=3)
manual_gradient = (probabilities - one_hot) / logits.shape[0]
```

This code constructs the same rows used in the manual trace. The MSE reference instead divides by M, the number of output elements across all axes; here M=2 and 2×([2, 4]−[1, 2])/2=[1, 2]. The unweighted mean binary reference also divides by M, not by an assumed batch count. Keep these fixture conditions explicit rather than applying the class-index formula to weighted or smoothed losses.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: CrossEntropyLoss expects unnormalized logits for the class-index case; BCEWithLogitsLoss also expects logits, not already-sigmoid inputs. MSE's same-shape contract must be checked rather than left to accidental broadcasting.

teaching_blocks.content:
For plain SGD with no momentum, weight decay or other modifications, let a parameter be 2, its current gradient 3 and learning rate 0.1. The reference new value is 2 − 0.1 × 3 = 1.7, with change −0.3. Clear old gradients, compute backward and then step. Initialize the optimizer with model.parameters() so it acts on the supplied trainable model parameters. A fixture that calls backward but never step would produce a gradient without this parameter update. Keep the plain-SGD restrictions visible so this arithmetic is not mistaken for the update rule of every optimizer.

Retain the current gradient separately from the observed parameter change. The former is produced by backward; the latter is produced by step acting on the parameters bound to the optimizer. A parameter change of −0.3 matches the plain-SGD reference for gradient 3 and rate 0.1, but the same number alone would not identify what happened if those inputs differed. Check before/after values and declared tolerances together. Clearing gradients before the next backward prevents previous contributions from altering the intended fresh-step reference. Keep this one-step verification bounded to the stated optimizer configuration rather than extending its equation to Adam.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
With five observations and retained batches of sizes 2, 2 and 1, compute model outputs and loss for each aligned feature/target pair. For every minibatch, zero gradients, backpropagate that batch's loss and apply the optimizer step. Collect scalar loss.item() values with batch counts, so an epoch summary does not pretend all batches contain two observations. In the deterministic plain-SGD fixture, retain the pre-step parameter and compare its observed change with −learning_rate × current_gradient under tolerance. Test the loop's supplied valid, boundary and failure cases. The repeated sequence is what links each batch to its intended current gradient, rather than using an accumulated leftover from another batch.

Loss aggregation needs the accompanying batch counts because the last one-observation batch does not contribute the same number of examples as a two-observation batch. Record each scalar with its batch size before applying the declared epoch-summary rule. The loop's nested structure is equally important: each epoch iterates its loader, and each minibatch performs the complete current-gradient update sequence. A step outside the intended minibatch position would define a different training procedure. The deterministic fixture can inspect one update within the loop, making the control flow and parameter-change evidence meet at the same minibatch.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: An epoch is not just a count of calls to step. Batch sizes affect how a loss summary is interpreted, and old gradients must not silently become part of the next minibatch's intended update.

Training mode and gradient recording can be considered independently in the fixture. Evaluation-mode dropout behaves as an identity even if graph recording is enabled. Training-mode dropout can still mask values while no_grad is active. Neither observation alone describes the whole validation procedure, which also excludes parameter updates. Inspect the layer output and the chosen context separately, then restore training mode before returning to the training loop. This avoids interpreting a stochastic dropout value as a prediction-quality problem or assuming that a disabled graph has also changed layer behavior.

media.group_title: Separate layer mode from gradient recording

segments.label: Training and validation use two separate controls
segments.summary: PyTorch's train and eval methods change the behavior of mode-sensitive layers such as dropout and batch normalization. Validation uses eval to select evaluation behavior and no_grad to prevent gradient-graph recording; these controls serve different purposes. Each training epoch starts in training mode and performs the forward pass, loss calculation, gradient clearing, backward pass, and optimizer step. The separate validation block switches to evaluation mode, disables graph recording, and computes validation loss without updating weights. Starting the next epoch in training mode restores training behavior.

context.concept_name: Stop training using validation behavior without consulting the protected test

coverage.learning_objective: Implement a validation-patience controller that returns the best retained model state.

required_facts.statement: Predeclare the validation quantity, improvement direction, minimum improvement and patience; patience counts consecutive epochs without sufficient improvement.
For a minimized validation quantity, reset the non-improvement counter only when current < best − min_delta; otherwise increment it and stop when the declared patience is exhausted.
Retain the model weights associated with the best monitored validation value rather than automatically using the last epoch’s weights.
A state_dict refers to live parameter values, so preserve a best-epoch state with a deep copy or a saved state file before later updates alter the model.
Do not use protected test observations to fit preprocessing, choose a model or tune its settings; doing so leaks information into the chosen system.
Implement the controller as a while loop bounded by maximum epochs and the non-improvement rule; update best loss/checkpoint inside the improvement branch and use break when patience is exhausted.
source_refs: python_tutorial#controlflow.html — Defining Functions; Default Argument Values; Keyword Arguments

teaching_blocks.title: Stop and Debug Training
teaching_blocks.content:
A validation quantity improves and then stalls. Early stopping is a predeclared controller over this sequence, not a decision to use whichever epoch happened to run last. Preserve the best checkpoint accepted under the declared minimum-improvement rule while training can still alter live parameters.

Source for checkpoint reference versus copy: [PyTorch Saving and Loading Models — Save/Load state_dict (Recommended), best_model_state note](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/saving_loading_models.html).

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Predeclare the validation quantity, improvement direction, minimum improvement and patience; patience counts consecutive epochs without sufficient improvement. For a minimized validation quantity, reset the non-improvement counter only when current < best − min_delta; otherwise increment it and stop when the declared patience is exhausted. Here, best is the validation value at the most recent checkpoint accepted under min_delta, not necessarily the lowest observed value. Retain that accepted checkpoint’s model weights rather than automatically using the last epoch’s weights.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content:
A state_dict refers to live parameter values, so preserve a best-epoch state with a deep copy or a saved state file before later updates alter the model. Do not use protected test observations to fit preprocessing, choose a model or tune its settings; doing so leaks information into the chosen system. Implement the controller as a while loop bounded by maximum epochs and the non-improvement rule; update best loss/checkpoint inside the improvement branch and use break when patience is exhausted.

Source for checkpoint reference versus copy: [PyTorch Saving and Loading Models — Save/Load state_dict (Recommended), best_model_state note](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/saving_loading_models.html).

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose minimized validation values are 0.50, 0.44, 0.43 and 0.45, with min_delta 0.02 and patience 2. The move from 0.50 to 0.44 is sufficient improvement and resets the counter. The value 0.43 does not satisfy 0.43 < 0.44−0.02, so the counter becomes one; 0.45 makes it two and exhausts patience. The lowest observed value is 0.43, but the best checkpoint accepted under min_delta is the one at 0.44. Preserve the 0.44 checkpoint’s weights by deep copy or a saved state file, and restore that checkpoint for subsequent use rather than the last weights. Protected-test observations do not decide patience or checkpoint choice.

Source for checkpoint reference versus copy: [PyTorch Saving and Loading Models — Save/Load state_dict (Recommended), best_model_state note](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/saving_loading_models.html).

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content:
A state_dict reference is not necessarily a frozen best-epoch snapshot. Later updates can alter live parameter values, and ‘slightly lower’ is not sufficient improvement when it fails the declared min_delta rule.

Source for checkpoint reference versus copy: [PyTorch Saving and Loading Models — Save/Load state_dict (Recommended), best_model_state note](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/saving_loading_models.html).

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the derivative reference predicts a negative gradient for a selected parameter, but the reproduced record shows zero. Inspect .grad after backward and before clearing it, then follow the derivative chain from loss through outputs to that parameter. Check the target representation and declared learning rate alongside the loss computation. Choose one supported root-cause hypothesis, apply its supplied correction and rerun the identical bounded fixture. Compare the corrected loss and gradient signs and magnitudes with the failing reference. A lower loss in a different task or with multiple simultaneous changes would not isolate this hypothesis. Keep assertion fixtures for both the expected computation and the reproduced failure.

The identical rerun is what makes the correction test informative. Preserve the fixture, target contract and baseline failing evidence while changing the one supported factor. If the correction is intended to restore a missing gradient path, inspect the derivative and parameter .grad at the same points as before. If the supplied cause concerns representation or learning rate, retain those resolved inputs in the comparison. Record whether the corrected bounded task meets its declared expectations, not just whether an exception disappeared. This isolates evidence for one hypothesis without claiming that all future training failures have the same cause.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A stalled loss does not justify arbitrary configuration changes. Gradient evidence has a timing requirement, and inspecting after zeroing gradients can hide the learning signal you intended to diagnose.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
For a linear layer with input width 20 and output width 10, the weight reference contains 200 elements and the bias 10. At four bytes each, those parameters alone account for 840 bytes, before gradients, activations and batch matrices are counted. Sum simultaneously live allocations using their own element widths. Inspect peak allocated and reserved evidence and whether saved diagnostics retain computation graphs. Change one supported factor, such as a smaller batch or removing an unnecessary retained graph reference, then rerun the same bounded task and verify completion and peak. Use scalar or detached diagnostic values where gradients through the saved values are not needed.

At the reproduced failure point, count only the allocations actually simultaneously live rather than adding every tensor ever created during the run. A saved graph-connected loss tensor can retain a computation reference; a scalar loss diagnostic does not need that gradient connection. Parameter element counts are another explicit component of the reference, alongside gradients, activations and batches. The allocated/reserved distinction then helps interpret the runtime observation. Verify the one supported correction against the same bounded workload and memory requirement, retaining the failed evidence for comparison rather than merely reporting that a smaller run completed.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: empty_cache cannot free storage occupied by live tensors. Reserved and allocated memory are different quantities, and counting only the input matrix cannot explain all live training memory.

CUDA work is asynchronous, so CPU clock timings require synchronization at the measurement boundaries to include completed accelerator work.

teaching_blocks.content: Wrap the measured computation in the PyTorch profiler context and mark data-loading and model-computation regions with record_function labels. teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: CUDA work is asynchronous, so CPU clock timings require synchronization at the measurement boundaries to include completed accelerator work. Change one supported bottleneck factor and compare the same bounded workload again rather than inferring improvement only from a code change. Inspect CPU and memory measurements and running process state during the profiled interval, using docker stats and docker top for a containerized run, to distinguish resource limits from stage timing evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Warm up the bounded workload, then profile its labeled regions. If the trace attributes most measured work to loading, test one supported loading factor rather than immediately changing model computation. Inspect CPU, memory and process state during the same interval; for the container fixture, docker stats and docker top provide that supporting evidence. After the change, compare the same bounded workload again without profiler overhead in the final timing. On CUDA, synchronize measurement boundaries so a CPU clock includes completed accelerator work. Keep the profiling attribution separate from the final unprofiled performance comparison, since they answer related but different questions.

The profiler trace supplies attribution, while the unprofiled rerun supplies the matched elapsed-time comparison. Keep the same bounded workload and one-factor change between those two comparisons. A loading-region label should enclose the intended loading work; a model-compute label should identify that separate work rather than blend it with setup. Runtime CPU, memory and process evidence must refer to the same window. Synchronization at accelerator timing boundaries accounts for asynchronous completion. This makes the observed difference interpretable without assuming that a profiler's overhead or a shifted measurement boundary is a genuine speed improvement.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A code change is not evidence of improvement. Asynchronous accelerator work and profiler overhead can alter timing interpretation unless the measurement boundaries and final comparison are controlled.

teaching_blocks.content:
For the bounded ViT image-classification adaptation, use these explicit imports:

```python
import torch
from torch import nn
from transformers import AutoImageProcessor, ViTForImageClassification, TrainingArguments, Trainer
``` Load the supplied compatible checkpoint with ViTForImageClassification.from_pretrained(checkpoint). Retain its original label mapping for the pretrained baseline before replacing the task head. Load the matching processor with AutoImageProcessor.from_pretrained(checkpoint). Calling that processor on images with return_tensors="pt" produces pixel_values; passing the resulting inputs as keyword arguments to the model yields logits through its .logits attribute. Use this same checkpoint processor for training and validation images rather than an unrelated representation. With the supplied preprocessed datasets and image collator, construct TrainingArguments with the declared output_dir, num_train_epochs, per_device_train_batch_size and learning_rate. Set eval_strategy="epoch" and remove_unused_columns=False. Construct Trainer with model, args, train_dataset, eval_dataset=validation_dataset, data_collator and processing_class=processor. Its train method executes the bounded supervised adaptation.

teaching_blocks.content: For classifier-only adaptation, iterate the existing model parameters and set their requires_grad to False. Then assign a new nn.Linear(model.config.hidden_size, num_labels) to model.classifier. Set model.num_labels and model.config.num_labels to num_labels and set config.id2label and config.label2id to the task maps. The newly constructed head parameters are trainable by default. Verify that head weights change while frozen backbone values do not. Evaluate the fine-tuned task predictions on the same validation cohort as the frozen pretrained output reference, without constructing an application or using protected test data. For binary validation counts, FPR = FP/(FP+TN) conditions on actual negatives, and FNR = FN/(FN+TP) conditions on actual positives; an empty conditioning group does not yield a defined rate.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine supplied training and validation images for two task classes. Retain the original pretrained mapping for the frozen baseline, and use the same checkpoint processor for image representation. Freeze existing parameters, replace the classifier with a two-output head using the hidden width, and update num_labels and both label maps. Verify logits shape (N, 2) and long target indices in [0, 2). In the adaptation run, inspect a selected head gradient against the chain-rule reference and verify changed head weights with unchanged frozen-backbone values. Compare adapted predictions with the frozen supplied reference on the same validation cohort under fixed cost and acceptance rules. Keep protected-test data outside adaptation and selection.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Freezing the old parameters does not freeze a newly constructed head by default. A changed head without a verified target mapping or matched validation comparison is not sufficient evidence of task-specific adaptation.

media.group_title: Separate direct execution from ordinary imports

segments.label: Guard a Python script’s entry point so imports do not invoke it
segments.summary: Python assigns __name__ the value "__main__" when a file runs directly and the module’s name when it is imported. Using two Python files, the demonstration first shows that unguarded top-level statements execute during import. It then moves the executable work into a main function and calls that function behind if __name__ == "__main__":. Direct execution still invokes main, but importing the file no longer invokes that guarded function. The guard controls the entry-point call; it does not prevent other top-level statements from executing during import.

bridge_note.before: Watch how __name__ changes between direct execution and import, then how guarding the main function changes the output. The example uses ordinary Python modules rather than a training task.
bridge_note.after: The clip establishes the entry-point guard. The text supplies parameter defaults and overrides, JSON configuration and records, notebook comparison, subprocess failure checks, f-string reporting, repository commits, and clean-shell output capture.

practice_anchor.objective: Convert the supplied notebook prototype into one executable training_script.py in the supplied repository. Write the imports and a training function with explicit parameters and defaults, keeping task state in parameters or local variables. Behind the entry-point guard, invoke training once with defaults and once with keyword overrides mapped from the declared JSON configuration. Emit resolved parameters and validation results with f-strings, serialize a run record, and recover its structured values. Save, stage, and commit the script. Run it from a clean shell with output redirection, inspect the captured output against the supplied notebook behavior, and verify a caller can execute it with subprocess.run using check=True.
practice_anchor.success: One committed script runs without notebook globals. Its captured output identifies the resolved parameters and validation result for both the default and configured calls, agrees with the supplied notebook behavior for corresponding settings, and has no execution errors. The JSON record reloads as structured values, ordinary import does not launch training, and the caller uses check=True to propagate a nonzero exit status.

coverage.learning_objective: Create and re-retrieve a hashed immutable dataset version despite an overwrite of latest.

required_facts.statement: A mutable object name can refer to new contents after an overwrite; Object Versioning retains noncurrent versions whose identities can be selected explicitly.

Retrieve a Google Cloud Storage snapshot with bucket.blob(object_name, generation=recorded_generation).download_to_filename(local_path), preserving the generation instead of resolving the current object.

Compute a digest from the actual bytes, for example hashlib.sha256(data_bytes).hexdigest(), and compare it with the recorded expected content identity.
Write the object name, generation and observed digest to the local snapshot record so later training can retrieve and verify the same bytes.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Upload the supplied dataset to the version-enabled test bucket and record its created generation and the SHA-256 digest of the local bytes. Later, select that recorded generation explicitly, verify it exists and download it. Compare the downloaded bytes' digest with the expected snapshot identity. In the authorized overwrite fixture, change only the mutable latest object, then retrieve the original generation again. The observed original digest should still match the snapshot record. Keep object name, generation and digest together: the name tells you which object family, the generation selects the version, and the digest checks the bytes you actually obtained.

The overwrite test separates immutable snapshot selection from the mutable object's current state. Verify the recorded generation exists before relying on it, and check the content after retrieval rather than assuming a version-qualified request returned the expected bytes. A local digest computed before upload and a digest of the later download can be compared directly as content evidence. Keep the selected generation in the record even when both old and latest objects happen to have the same name. The test proves retrieval of the recorded fixture, not a claim that mutable names are intrinsically safe for reproduction.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A mutable object name is not immutable data identity. Recording a digest without verifying downloaded bytes also does not establish that the intended snapshot was retrieved.

video_need.reason: A live fixture with visible intermediate state and acceptance checks would make this distinction concrete: Reproducibility requires exact data identity, not a mutable location.

Retrieve that generation and verify its digest, then repeat the retrieval and verification after overwriting the mutable latest object in the authorized fixture.

Downloads explicitly select the recorded generation and match the recorded digest both before and after the mutable latest object changes.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Inspect the local HEAD, collect pinned dependency versions with pip freeze, and record sys.version and sys.executable with the supplied runtime identity. Serialize that dictionary to the declared text manifest and parse it back. Compare the parsed revision, dependency mapping and runtime identity with independently inspected values. If the manifest says revision A but HEAD is B, reject the match rather than correcting the observed revision to fit the manifest. The dependency file can be installed with pip install -r in the declared environment. Keep the saved manifest and verified values identifiable so a later reproduction can resolve the recorded context.

The parsed manifest is the artifact a later execution will read, so inspect it after serialization rather than only inspecting the in-memory dictionary that preceded writing. Compare its dependency mapping with the freeze output, its revision with HEAD and its Python/runtime fields with the actual process. Paths such as sys.executable help identify which interpreter executed, while sys.version records that interpreter's version information. Keep these values beside the environment identity instead of treating them as substitutes for it. A mismatch is a verification failure to resolve, not a reason to change the independently observed environment values.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Writing a manifest is not verifying it. Runtime details and dependency pins must come from the actual environment, and a parsed record with a mismatch cannot be declared accurate.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Retrieve the run's commit and dataset generation. Check out and verify the recorded local commit, download and verify the recorded snapshot, and use the pinned Python/dependency environment. Resolve defaults and keyword overrides through the execution function's parameters. Navigate to the recorded directories before resolving relative script or artifact paths, then launch a clean subprocess with captured output and checked exit status. Inspect the captured result rather than assuming launch means completion. In a failure fixture, a changed latest dataset or different working directory should be distinguishable from the recorded execution context. A shell pipe connects one command's output to another's input; it is not the same operation as saving both output streams to a log.

Compare captured resolved parameters with the run record as well as inspecting exit success. A process can exit successfully while using a wrong dataset or default setting, so the reproduction verdict needs identity and configuration checks too. Relative paths are interpreted from the actual working directory; navigate explicitly before invoking the recorded script. The pinned environment and recorded code commit govern which implementation runs, while the verified snapshot governs its inputs. These separate pieces make the bounded reproduction auditable instead of relying on an operator's memory of the previous notebook session.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: The same script filename is not reproduction identity. A changed revision, mutable dataset or unresolved local path can change the executed experiment despite a familiar name.

context.concept_name: Evaluate the frozen selected model and threshold against the baseline on the protected test set

coverage.learning_objective: Evaluate the frozen selected candidate on protected test observations without retuning.

required_facts.statement: Only evaluate the protected test set after fixing the selected candidate, fitted preprocessing and decision threshold; test results must not choose a replacement candidate or threshold.
Generate selected-model and baseline predictions for the same protected-test observations and compare the precommitted predictive quantities on that cohort.

required_facts.statement: For binary validation counts, FPR = FP/(FP+TN) conditions on actual negatives, and FNR = FN/(FN+TP) conditions on actual positives; an empty conditioning group does not yield a defined rate.
source_refs: google_ml_crash_course#classification/accuracy-precision-recall — Accuracy; Recall, or true positive rate; False positive rate; Precision

required_facts.statement: With zero cost for correct predictions and supplied deployment class probabilities, expected error cost is P(Y=0) × FPR × cost_FP + P(Y=1) × FNR × cost_FN.

teaching_blocks.title: Evaluate the Frozen Choice
teaching_blocks.content: The protected test is the final comparison for the already fixed system. Freeze candidate, preprocessing and threshold first; a disappointing test result must be reported rather than used to choose a replacement.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Only evaluate the protected test set after fixing the selected candidate, fitted preprocessing and decision threshold; test results must not choose a replacement candidate or threshold. teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: For binary validation counts, FPR = FP/(FP+TN) conditions on actual negatives, and FNR = FN/(FN+TP) conditions on actual positives; an empty conditioning group does not yield a defined rate. With zero cost for correct predictions and supplied deployment class probabilities, expected error cost is P(Y=0) × FPR × cost_FP + P(Y=1) × FNR × cost_FN.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose validation selected candidate B and its threshold, and the protected cohort contains a different observed class mix. Predict that cohort with B and the baseline on the same observations. Use the already fixed deployment probabilities and error costs, not new values chosen to make B pass. Check the precommitted quality and operating requirements and retain the test's actual-class conditioning counts. If B fails the requirement, report failure. A threshold adjustment based on these test outcomes would let the protected observations choose the system, contradicting the boundary. The output is a final matched comparison, not another candidate-selection round.

Freeze means the choices are made before test outcomes are observed: model identity, fitted preprocessing, threshold, metric inputs and requirements all retain their declared values. The baseline and candidate predictions then use the same protected observations for a final matched comparison. Retain the test's observed conditioning counts while applying the supplied deployment probabilities; these are different roles in the calculation. If a required quantity is undefined or a requirement fails, report that outcome explicitly. This protects the interpretation of final testing rather than using it as a source of additional tuning information.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Protected testing is not a second tuning opportunity. Test failure does not authorize switching candidate, refitting preprocessing or searching for a better threshold on those observations.

Verify each selected input version. If the API only accepts a mutable channel URI, materialize the selected version at the controlled immutable location rather than inventing a version argument. The container reads the supplied channel beneath /opt/ml/input/data and writes its model under /opt/ml/model. Inspect terminal status, failure reason when present and the returned artifact location. Retrieve the artifact with the authorized storage client and compare its reference with the completed job record. Keep snapshot, code/configuration and run/artifact identities together.

teaching_blocks.content: Job submission is not completion, and an input name is not verified input identity. Managed resources are released after termination; confirm terminal status rather than assuming the request already ended compute use.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the request contract permits a two-feature matrix with one row per order. A body decoding to three rows of two permitted values can be checked for rank and width, then the response must have the declared row alignment. A body missing a required key fails before prediction. A numeric boundary fixture can test an included limit and a value just beyond it. Send the serialized body as encoded bytes with the declared JSON header and a bounded timeout, decode the returned JSON and inspect its fields. Parsing success, request validity and response correctness are three different checks; retain each failure explicitly rather than returning a successful result for malformed input.

The schema checks must happen before using a field as model input. Check that the required key exists, that its value has the declared type and that its dimensions and values satisfy the stated predicates. A missing key and an out-of-range value are different rejected fixtures. After prediction, inspect the structured response independently: required output keys, row correspondence and declared value or shape expectations. Bounded request timing is part of the fixture transport, not a substitute for contract validation. Explicit rejection distinguishes invalid input from a successful prediction containing the wrong data.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Raw JSON text is not the structured request, and successful JSON decoding is not schema acceptance. A response with the wrong row correspondence still violates the prediction contract.

video_need.reason: A live fixture with visible intermediate state and acceptance checks would make this distinction concrete: Schemas constrain structural exchange boundaries separately from prediction execution.

A response with incorrect output fields or row alignment is detected independently. Requests use encoded JSON bytes, the declared header and a stated timeout; responses are decoded before validation.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
In do_POST, read the declared body length from headers and then those bytes from rfile. Decode and validate the request before applying fitted preprocessing and the model, without fit or parameter updates. Encode the named response dictionary as UTF-8 JSON. Write the status and headers, finish the headers and write the body to wfile. Configure the supplied HTTPServer host and port, and exercise the valid, boundary and invalid fixtures. Trace one request through bytes, structured fields, validated model input and encoded output. This keeps request transport and prediction state separate rather than letting every request alter the model.

The byte length describes the encoded response, so compute it from the body actually written rather than from an assumed count of characters. JSON serialization and UTF-8 encoding belong before the response headers that describe that body. On input, Content-Length governs the declared read boundary, while schema checks govern whether decoded content is permitted. Fitted prediction state remains separate from transport handling. The fixture should show a complete bounded request/response exchange with explicit validation, status, headers and body, without turning the standard-library demonstration into a broader production-service design.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose five keyed orders are processed in chunks of two, two and one. Apply the fitted preprocessing and model to each chunk, keeping each order key with its prediction. Write that bounded set of serialized results before reading the next chunk. Decode the written fixture again and verify its schema and one-result-per-eligible-key correspondence. A missing key or duplicate output is a failure even if the total number of rows looks reasonable. Keep explicit input and output handles and the declared reader format. The procedure is inference over chunks, not fitting a new model or preprocessor for whichever chunk happens to arrive next.

Keep an output key beside its prediction through serialization, not merely in a temporary input structure. After writing, decode the fixture and compare key coverage against the eligible input IDs. A duplicate result for A plus a missing result for B could leave the total row count unchanged, which is why correspondence needs more than counting rows. Each chunk uses the same fitted objects and declared response schema. The bounded writer and reader handles establish where results were produced and re-inspected. This completes an inference path whose correctness includes persistence and identity, not only in-memory prediction values.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A matching total row count does not guarantee one result for every eligible input key. Batch inference preserves keys and fitted state, rather than relying on incidental output order.

Decoded output follows the declared schema and contains exactly one prediction per eligible order key. Assertions pass for valid and boundary fixtures and raise AssertionError for declared failures, including duplicate output keys paired with missing keys despite an unchanged total count.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose one request starts at time 1.0, waits until 1.4 for its batch and completes at 1.6. Its end-to-end duration is 0.6 seconds, not the 0.2-second post-wait interval. Decode the successful response and associate it with the request identity and batching setting. Compute the declared tail percentile, mean and specified spread over the eligible successful-response durations in one unit. Compare settings using the same trace and population interpretation, then choose only a limit satisfying the supplied latency objective. Keep the successful-response sample count visible rather than treating a duration list as if it included failures or unmatched responses.

Use a timeline for the same identified request to avoid measuring different intervals under different settings. Start-to-response timing includes the waiting interval, and the selected successful-response population determines which durations enter the percentile. Record the sample count, units and percentile convention so the numerical summary is reproducible. A limit that reduces model-execution time but increases waiting may fail the full latency objective. The supplied trace is evidence about those measured settings and eligible responses; it does not authorize inventing an unmeasured batching configuration or treating unmatched responses as valid duration samples.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Batch waiting belongs in the stated end-to-end latency. A faster execution interval alone does not make a batching limit acceptable under the full request objective.

teaching_blocks.content: For a fixed Compose scaling fixture, declare deploy.replicas or use docker compose up -d --scale SERVICE=COUNT, then inspect the actual replica count. A target-tracking scaling policy specifies a metric, target value and scale-in/scale-out cooldowns; apply only the supported supplied policy to the existing scalable target.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Compare scale settings at the same declared load and select capacity that meets observed success, p99 latency and throughput requirements rather than assuming more replicas are always better. Estimate client-visible success probability as successful eligible attempts divided by all eligible attempts in the defined measurement window, counting failed attempts in the denominator. Compute the declared tail-latency percentile with np.percentile(completed_latency_values, declared_percentile), retaining its convention, sample count and time unit.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Measure completed successful requests divided by elapsed measurement time for successful throughput, and compare it with the offered load rather than equating arrivals with completed work. teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Restore the nonproduction runtime’s original replica and lifecycle settings after the bounded scaling check. Compute the arithmetic mean with np.mean(numeric_values) over the selected numeric observations. Compute standard deviation with np.std(numeric_values, ddof=0), which divides squared deviations by N before taking the square root; use ddof=1 only when the stated calculation requires the N−1 divisor.

teaching_blocks.title: Gate Data and Model Releases
teaching_blocks.content: A model release needs a gate over its exact evidence and predeclared requirements. Aggregate improvement is not a substitute for all required quality and operating predicates being complete and passing.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: A release gate compares the candidate with the accepted reference and the predeclared quality requirements before promotion. Read the supplied candidate evidence fields, evaluate each required acceptance predicate and report which predicate failed when the verdict is reject. Calculate validation expected error cost using the predeclared deployment probabilities and error costs, and include the fixed latency/operating limits in eligibility.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: A failed or incomplete required gate blocks promotion rather than being treated as success. For binary validation counts, FPR = FP/(FP+TN) conditions on actual negatives, and FNR = FN/(FN+TP) conditions on actual positives; an empty conditioning group does not yield a defined rate. With zero cost for correct predictions and supplied deployment class probabilities, expected error cost is P(Y=0) × FPR × cost_FP + P(Y=1) × FNR × cost_FN.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Do not use protected test observations to fit preprocessing, choose a model or tune its settings; doing so leaks information into the chosen system. In an existing Cloud Build YAML/JSON configuration, each steps item declares its execution image in name and its command in args or script; wire the function/test entry point into the assigned stage. Assign step IDs and set waitFor to the required preceding step IDs; downstream execution depends on those steps completing successfully, not just their textual location.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the candidate's expected cost is below the permitted bound but its fixed latency check fails. Return reject with that predicate identified, rather than reporting the cost success as release approval. Calculate cost with the fixed class probabilities and supplied error costs, retaining actual-class denominators. Bind the evidence to the candidate identity. In the existing event-triggered build, configure the gate's image, command and waitFor edges, without failure-tolerant settings. Inspect actual resolved inputs and stage results for accepted and rejected events. Protected-test observations remain outside fitting and tuning; an incomplete required gate blocks promotion just as a failed one does.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A release gate is not an average of independent requirements. One failed or incomplete required condition blocks promotion even when another metric improves.

video_need.reason: A live fixture with visible intermediate state and acceptance checks would make this distinction concrete: A release gate fails closed on model acceptance evidence before promotion.

practice_anchor.objective: Write a learner-defined Python acceptance function and its required imports within the supplied artifact-triggered release pipeline. Failing or incomplete evidence identifies the affected predicate, raises an explicit exception, and produces an unsuccessful gate process with no promotion. Assertions pass, the configuration retains fatal failure behavior and explicit step dependencies, and actual run results and resolved inputs confirm both outcomes.

context.concept_name: Monitor production input and prediction distributions

coverage.learning_objective: Summarize aligned reference and production input/output distributions over a defined window.

required_facts.statement: Compare captured production inputs with the defined reference dataset using the same feature representations, reference constraints and measurement window.
For numerical values, np.histogram(values, bins=fixed_edges) returns bin counts; divide by the eligible observation count to compare bin proportions on the same edges.
For categorical or predicted-class values, count each declared category and divide by its window total, retaining category definitions and the total count.
Record the production window, reference identity and observed summaries so an apparent distribution change can be investigated.
Compute the arithmetic mean with np.mean(numeric_values) over the selected numeric observations.

Compute standard deviation with np.std(numeric_values, ddof=0), which divides squared deviations by N before taking the square root; use ddof=1 only when the stated calculation requires the N−1 divisor.

teaching_blocks.title: Monitor Distributions and Drift
teaching_blocks.content: Production-input summaries need a defined reference and measurement window. Compare the same representations and categories so an apparent change is not merely the result of different bins or different denominators.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Compare captured production inputs with the defined reference dataset using the same feature representations, reference constraints and measurement window. For numerical values, np.histogram(values, bins=fixed_edges) returns bin counts; divide by the eligible observation count to compare bin proportions on the same edges. For categorical or predicted-class values, count each declared category and divide by its window total, retaining category definitions and the total count.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Record the production window, reference identity and observed summaries so an apparent distribution change can be investigated. Compute standard deviation with np.std(numeric_values, ddof=0), which divides squared deviations by N before taking the square root; use ddof=1 only when the stated calculation requires the N−1 divisor.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the reference has category counts 60 and 40, while the production window has counts 30 and 70, each out of 100. Their aligned proportions are [0.60, 0.40] and [0.30, 0.70]. For numerical features, use the same fixed histogram edges and divide each window's counts by its eligible observation count. Record reference identity, production window and selected means and standard deviations with the specified divisor. A 200-observation window needs its own denominator, not the reference total. This record supports investigation of a distribution change; it does not yet claim that labeled prediction errors increased.

Fixed bins make numerical proportions refer to the same intervals in both windows. The eligible denominator also matters if values outside the declared eligible set are handled explicitly by the reference constraints. For categories, preserve declared category definitions and count every declared category so an absent current category still has a position in the aligned comparison. Means and standard deviations describe selected numerical observations with their specified divisor. Retain these summaries together with window and reference identity. That record supports investigating what distribution changed without silently redefining the measurement between reference and production.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Different bins or category mappings can make distributions incomparable. Keep the same representation and each window's own eligible count instead of comparing raw counts alone.

context.concept_name: Distinguish data drift, concept drift and observed quality degradation

coverage.learning_objective: Distinguish input shift, changed target relationship and label-supported quality degradation.

required_facts.statement: Input data drift is a change in the observed input distribution relative to its reference; input drift monitoring alone does not measure labeled prediction quality.
Concept drift changes the conditional target relationship P(Y|X), that is, the relationship between features and labels; a previously useful model can become less useful as that relationship changes.
Observed model quality degradation requires comparing predictions with corresponding ground-truth labels and the declared quality reference.
Without matched available labels, report the supported distribution or service evidence and the unresolved quality question rather than asserting labeled quality degradation.
source_refs: sagemaker_model_monitor#model-monitor-model-quality-merge.html — Ingest Ground Truth labels and merge them with predictions

required_facts.statement: Input marginals describe P(X), conditional-target evidence describes P(Y|X), and matched-label errors describe observed quality; changing one does not logically establish changes in all three.

teaching_blocks.title: Monitor Distributions and Drift
teaching_blocks.content: An input distribution changed, but labels are not yet available. Distinguish evidence about inputs, evidence about the conditional target relationship and measured prediction quality before deciding what the observation supports.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Input data drift is a change in the observed input distribution relative to its reference; input drift monitoring alone does not measure labeled prediction quality. Concept drift changes the conditional target relationship P(Y|X), that is, the relationship between features and labels; a previously useful model can become less useful as that relationship changes. Observed model quality degradation requires comparing predictions with corresponding ground-truth labels and the declared quality reference.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Without matched available labels, report the supported distribution or service evidence and the unresolved quality question rather than asserting labeled quality degradation. Input marginals describe P(X), conditional-target evidence describes P(Y|X), and matched-label errors describe observed quality; changing one does not logically establish changes in all three.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose a production window contains more long-distance orders than the reference. That is evidence about P(X), the input distribution. It does not establish that P(Y|X), the target relationship conditional on features, changed. To claim observed quality degradation, compare predictions with their corresponding ground truth and the declared quality reference. If matched available labels are absent, record the supported distribution or service observation and the unresolved quality question. Conversely, a conditional target relationship can change in the concept-drift sense even when an input summary is not the evidence that reveals it. Keep the three questions distinct rather than calling every change ‘the model got worse.’

Separate an operational report into what is observed and what is unresolved. More long-distance inputs support an input-distribution statement. Matched labels compared with the quality reference support an observed-error statement. Conditional-target evidence addresses whether the feature/label relationship changed. The absence of labels does not prove that quality stayed constant; it means the labeled-quality question is not yet measured by that evidence. Likewise, input drift does not prove that quality worsened. Keeping these distinctions preserves uncertainty without discarding useful distribution or service evidence, and prevents a response justified by one type of evidence from being mislabeled as another.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Input drift alone is not labeled quality degradation. Changes in P(X), P(Y|X) and matched-label errors do not logically establish one another.

State that each observation alone does not establish the other two changes, and that labeled quality remains unresolved when matched labels are unavailable.

context.concept_name: Detect model-input data drift against a defined reference distribution

coverage.learning_objective: Detect a defined feature-distribution difference using aligned proportions and numeric summaries.

Compute standard deviation with np.std(numeric_values, ddof=0), which divides squared deviations by N before taking the square root; use ddof=1 only when the stated calculation requires the N−1 divisor.

teaching_blocks.content: Define the reference feature distribution, comparison window and declared drift criterion before checking production data. teaching_blocks.content: A drift detection result indicates a distribution difference under that rule, not by itself a measured increase in target prediction error. teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Compute each category’s reference/current count divided by its own window total, then apply the supplied probability-distance equation and threshold to aligned category vectors.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose aligned category proportions are [0.60, 0.40] in the reference and [0.30, 0.70] in the current window. Apply the supplied probability-distance equation and threshold to those vectors, retaining each window's eligible total. Do not invent a distance rule if the task supplies one. For numerical features, keep fixed bin edges and the required mean/spread interpretation. Report which features cross the declared rule together with reference identity and comparison window. The verdict identifies a distribution difference under that criterion; it does not report an increase in target error without corresponding labeled-quality evidence.

The same reference/current vectors can give a decision only under the declared distance or significance rule. Record the equation's resolved inputs and criterion beside its verdict, rather than showing a bare alert with no comparison definition. Each window's proportions use its own eligible total, so unequal sample sizes do not mean raw count differences are themselves the drift quantity. Numerical summaries retain the stated mean and spread conventions. Report feature-level crossings under that rule and preserve the separate question of labeled model quality. This makes the detection reproducible without claiming a causal performance effect.

teaching_blocks.content: A drift threshold crossing is not proof that prediction error increased. Also, different category mappings or reused reference denominators would change the comparison rather than measure the intended distributions.

teaching_blocks.content:

Calculate both costs with the same supplied deployment probabilities, error costs and actual-class conditional rates. A missing conditioning group does not provide a defined rate. Keep protected-test observations out of fitting and setting choice. Bind the exact registry/artifact identity and verdict to the controlled promotion record, with assertion fixtures for accepted, boundary and failed cases. Approval evidence for candidate A must not be reused for candidate B just because both came from the same retraining pipeline.

The incumbent and candidate must be evaluated under the same fixed validation question before their expected costs are comparable. Reconnect and inspect the restored model service. Verify readiness and a bounded prediction exchange against the expected contract rather than assuming a running VM means recovery. The pre-recovery evidence is important because stop/start can change process state and remove the immediate fault symptom. Inspect the authorized instance before acting, record what failed and test the runbook's supported hypothesis. After start completes, reconnect and compare model-service state and endpoint behavior with the expected contract. A running instance state is a lifecycle observation; readiness and a successful bounded prediction are service observations. Retain both in the same recovery record along with authorized target identity. This verifies the supplied recovery procedure without assuming that a restart of an arbitrary resource would be safe or sufficient.

For a containerized process, compare docker top evidence with the recorded running workload identity. Do not silently append an unrelated stopped interval to lower the apparent utilization. The result is descriptive CPU/memory evidence with units and process identity, not an execution-cost calculation.

Resource samples need both units and identity. CPU percent and memory units are not interchangeable columns, and their descriptive summaries should cover the same matched workload interval. The lifecycle record helps distinguish a stopped instance from an active measurement window. Process inspection adds evidence that the workload named in the report was actually running. Keep observation counts visible for both series and use the stated standard-deviation divisor. These summaries characterize resource usage during the bounded task; they do not independently establish billed cost, request success or model quality.

teaching_blocks.title: Control Workload Cost and Retire Resources
teaching_blocks.content: Workload expenditure includes attributable direct and shared billing rows, not just time a training VM was computing. Select workload identities and reporting windows, then reconcile every eligible amount.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Billing reports associate charges with services, resources and time intervals; select the declared training/inference workload and reporting window before comparing expenditure. Use the existing workload labels or resource-to-workload mapping to connect billed resource usage with the run or serving workload. Stopping a VM can end compute charges while persistent disks and other resources remain billable, so compute time alone does not account for all workload expenditure.

teaching_blocks.content: Aggregate the supplied charge records by workload and charge category and reconcile the attributed total with the eligible record total. Calculate a declared unit-cost quantity from attributed expenditure divided by the corresponding completed work, retaining both the billing and work-measurement windows. Start and connect to both tagged instances for their bounded training/inference workloads, record their separate lifecycle windows, and stop both after execution.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Allocate direct billing rows to the matching tagged workload/lifecycle interval and shared rows under the supplied explicit sharing rule, retaining shared charges instead of dropping them. Sum allocations per window, flag unusually large or unmatched allocations, and check that all allocated plus explicitly unallocated amounts reconcile to the eligible billing-export total. For an authorized supplied Compute Engine VM, gcloud compute instances start INSTANCE --zone=ZONE and gcloud compute instances stop INSTANCE --zone=ZONE change its lifecycle state; wait for the operation and inspect the resulting state.

teaching_blocks.content: Connect to the running authorized VM with gcloud compute ssh INSTANCE --zone=ZONE to execute the workload. Use gcloud compute instances describe INSTANCE --zone=ZONE to inspect the instance status and identity before and after the authorized lifecycle action. Compute the arithmetic mean with np.mean(numeric_values) over the selected numeric observations.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Compute standard deviation with np.std(numeric_values, ddof=0), which divides squared deviations by N before taking the square root; use ddof=1 only when the stated calculation requires the N−1 divisor.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose direct charges are 6 for training and 4 for inference, with a shared charge of 2 allocated equally under the supplied rule. The allocations are 7 and 5, summing to the eligible total 12. If inference completed 100 eligible predictions in the matching work window, its declared unit cost is 5/100 = 0.05. Keep direct lifecycle windows and shared allocation rules visible; stopped compute may still have persistent disk charges. Start and connect to both tagged test instances for bounded execution, then stop and inspect both. Flag unmatched or unusually large allocations and reconcile allocated plus explicitly unallocated amounts against the billing-export total.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Compute duration alone is not all workload expenditure. Shared charges cannot disappear from reconciliation, and unit cost needs the corresponding completed-work denominator and measurement window.

video_need.reason: A live fixture with visible intermediate state and acceptance checks would make this distinction concrete: Attribution binds expenditure to accountable workload identity.

practice_anchor.objective: Inspect, start and connect to two supplied authorized tagged training/inference instances. Execute the supplied bounded workloads, record separate lifecycle windows, then stop and inspect both instances. Allocate the supplied billing export by workload, charge category and window using the existing mapping and explicit shared-charge rule. Calculate the mean and standard deviation of per-window attributed costs, flag unusual or unmatched allocations, and reconcile the export.
practice_anchor.success: Both instances have recorded identities, lifecycle windows and verified stopped states. Direct charges match the supplied workload mapping and applicable intervals; shared and persistent-resource charges remain accounted for. Per-window totals, arithmetic mean and population standard deviation are correct. Unusual and unmatched allocations are flagged, and allocated plus explicitly unallocated amounts equal the eligible export total.

live_code.required_skill: Use authorized instance lifecycle and connection commands, apply supplied billing-allocation rules, and calculate NumPy summary statistics over per-window costs.
allowed_syntax: np.std(numeric_values, ddof=1) only when the supplied calculation explicitly requires the N−1 divisor
Variable assignment, numeric literals, indexing and basic arithmetic
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide two authorized existing instances identified as training and inference, their zones and existing workload labels or mapping, supplied bounded execution commands, and a lifecycle-record template. Supply billing rows with service, resource, time interval, charge category and amount; the reporting window, explicit sharing rule, and unusual-allocation criterion are declared. Use the illustrative direct charges of 6 for training and 4 for inference and a shared charge of 2 split equally.
live_code.observable_success: The lifecycle record shows both instances inspected before and after authorized actions, connected while running, and stopped after execution. The allocation ledger produces training and inference totals of 7 and 5 for the illustrative window. For numeric_values containing those two costs, np.mean returns 6 and np.std with ddof=0 returns 1. The ledger retains shared charges, records any unmatched amounts explicitly, applies the supplied unusual-allocation criterion, and reconciles to the eligible total of 12.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the allocation ledger visible alongside the separate training and inference lifecycle windows: billed resource and interval, workload mapping, charge category, direct or shared allocation rule, attributed amount and any explicitly unallocated amount. Show per-window totals, mean, standard deviation, anomaly flags and the reconciliation to the eligible export total.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content: Write the supplied workload scope, period and thresholds and bind the existing Pub/Sub notification path to the permitted response pipeline.
